data.content_ref: inline:{"analogy":null,"claim":"Suppression versus efficiency can be distinguished by examining the failure modes of the owning lineage. If it is efficiency, failures will be 'depth-limit' (local optima). If it is suppression, failures will be 'vocab-limit' (un-expressible). In a single run, suppression is evidenced by problems where the owning lineage generates no candidate at all, or only tautological ones, while a rival lineage\u2014given the same problem\u2014immediately produces a non-trivial candidate.","counterconditions":[{"case":"Vocab-limit failures are indistinguishable from extreme depth-limit failures where all non-tautological candidates are pruned.","eval":"observation"},{"case":"Rival lineages always produce non-trivial candidates for any problem, making the test trivially true and non-discriminating.","eval":"observation"},{"case":"The system never allows rival lineages to attempt the same problem, making the counterfactual unobservable in a single run.","eval":"observation"}],"definitions":[],"derivation":[],"formalization_refs":[],"mechanism":"Efficiency implies a rational trade-off: the chosen path (within-lineage) is the most cost-effective, and failure occurs when the problem is too hard for any lineage. Suppression implies an artificial constraint: the chosen path is incapable of expressing the solution, even if the solution is easily expressible in another path. The distinguishing mechanism is the expressibility gap. If the owning lineage fails because it lacks the computational resources to explore its own space, that is efficiency. If it fails because its space does not contain the solution concept, that is suppression.","premises":[],"schema":"deepreason-reasoning-envelope-v1","scope":{"covers":[],"excludes":[]},"simulation_refs":[],"uncertainties":[]}
